title: 2026 State of Reliability: Assessment Overview of 2025 Bulk Power System Performance
date_evidence:
2026 State of Reliability 
Assessment Overview of 2025 Bulk Power System Performance
June 24, 2026
key_claim: Conventional generation weighted equivalent forced outage rate rose to 9.2% in 2025 against historical norms rarely exceeding 8%, driven by coal and combined-cycle units, and NERC recommends that reserve requirements be adjusted to account for lower conventional generation availability.
frame_summary: NERC is arguing that bulk-power-system risk has shifted from single contingencies to correlated, system-wide stresses, and that the declining availability of an ageing combustion fleet is eroding deployable reserves faster than headline capacity registers show.
verbatim_quote: These mandates do improve system capacity, but that capacity may not be from reliable units.
verbatim_list:
The report identifies a meaningful increase in conventional generator forced outage rates in 2025, 
with annual weighted equivalent forced outage rates (WEFOR) increasing to 9.2% compared to 
historical norms rarely exceeding 8%.

Coal and combined-cycle units were the primary drivers of this 
increase with an increase of over 39.8 TWh and 19.1 TWh of unavailable energy year over year,
respectively.

NERC and the relevant stakeholders should consider adjusting or at least be prepared to adjust 
reserve requirements to account for lower conventional generation availability.

Most large coal units are over 40 years old and are expected to be retired in the relatively near 
future.
notes: Primary anchor for the availability-decline mechanism. NERC's own caveat on 202(c) mandates is the load-bearing line for this scan.

title: U.S. coal-fired generating capacity retired in 2025 was the least in 15 years
date_evidence:
In-brief analysis

April 13, 2026

# [U.S. coal-fired generating capacity retired in 2025 was the least in 15 years](#)
key_claim: Only 2.6 GW of US coal capacity retired in 2025 against 8.5 GW planned, with 4.8 GW of planned retirements delayed to a future year and a further 1.1 GW cancelled outright.
frame_summary: EIA is arguing that scheduled coal retirement has stalled, and documents emergency orders and owner decisions as the mechanisms pushing closure dates into later years rather than cancelling the underlying trend.
verbatim_quote: During 2025, the U.S. electric power sector retired 2.6 gigawatts (GW) of coal-fired generating capacity at four power plants, the least since 2010.
verbatim_list: At the beginning of 2025, coal plant operators had planned to retire 8.5 GW of capacity; however, 4.8 GW of planned retirements were delayed to a future year, and the operators of two coal plants (1.1 GW) cancelled plans to retire.
notes: Canonical primary dataset for the size of the deferred cohort. title: New ICF Report Finds U.S. Has Just 3% Excess Generating Capacity as Electricity Demand Accelerates
date_evidence: RESTON, Va. (June 25, 2026) — ICF (NASDAQ:ICFI), a leading global solutions and technology provider, today released a new report on rising U.S. electricity demand
key_claim: The US power system holds only about 26 GW of excess generating capacity above minimum resource adequacy requirements, roughly 3% of total capacity, and ERCOT and PJM have none.
frame_summary: ICF is arguing that the binding question has moved from how fast demand grows to how fast generation, transmission and grid infrastructure can be built, and that a 3% cushion leaves no tolerance for delivery slippage.
verbatim_quote: The report also found that ERCOT and PJM, the nation’s fastest-growing electricity markets, have no excess generating capacity available to reliably support additional demand growth.
verbatim_list: The report, Electricity demand growth: How will the grid keep pace?, finds that the U.S. power system currently has only about 26 GW of excess generating capacity above minimum resource adequacy requirements, which is roughly 3% of total capacity.
A 3% capacity cushion leaves little room for error.

title: Review of NERC's 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment
key_claim: Supplementing NERC's 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment with Lawrence Berkeley National Lab queue data, every region including the two NERC flagged as elevated risk is resource adequate under extreme conditions, with 5% to 93% more reserves than target.
frame_summary: Grid Strategies is arguing that NERC's assessments understate available reserves by excluding likely-to-connect queue resources, non-firm imports and operational mitigations, so the reliability risk is smaller than the headline assessment implies.
verbatim_quote: However, this latest analysis by Grid Strategies, which supplements NERC’s SRA with reputable queue data from the Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, suggests the two regions are also resource adequate under extreme conditions.
verbatim_list: This more comprehensive picture of likely-to-connect resources—plus non-firm imports from neighboring regions and operational mitigation strategies—enables all regions to have between 5% – 93% *more* reserves than their target reserve margin.

title: The Queue Before the Queue: GEV's Backlog Extends to 2031
key_claim: GE Vernova's gas turbine backlog reached 116 GW in Q2 2026 and is sold out to 2031, while operating gas plants transact at roughly half of replacement cost, tilting the build-versus-buy decision toward keeping existing assets.
frame_summary: Enverus is arguing that equipment scarcity has made retaining or acquiring existing generation the rational commercial choice over new build, which is the economic logic underneath retirement deferral.
verbatim_quote: Operational assets continue to transact at approximately half of replacement costs.
verbatim_list: GEV’s gas turbine backlog climbed to 116 GW in Q2, up from 100 GW in the prior quarter as utilities, independent power producers (IPPs) and data center developers continue securing generation equipment years in advance.

title: Power plants under DOE emergency orders are producing way less energy than before
key_claim: Five plants held open under DOE emergency orders produced 1.5 million MWh in Q1 2026, down 65% year on year, with individual capacity factors well below their four-year averages and repair bills mounting.
frame_summary: Utility Dive is arguing, from EIA generation data, that the emergency orders are not delivering the output their grid-emergency justification implies, because the plants being held open were already being run down for closure.
verbatim_quote: Combined, five of the power plants produced 1.5 million MWh in the first quarter of this year under the DOE’s orders, down 65% from the 4.3 million MWh they generated in the same period last year.
verbatim_list: Since the orders were issued, Consumers Energy’s 1,420-MW Campbell power in Michigan has run at a 46% capacity factor since June 1, down from a nearly 66% average in the same periods in the previous four years, EIA data shows.
NIPSCO’s 847-MW Schahfer units in Indiana ran at a 17% capacity factor in the first quarter this year, down from an average of 24% in the first three months in the previous four years.

CenterPoint’s 104-MW F.B. Culley Unit 2 operated at a 14% capacity factor in its first three months under its DOE order, down from an average of nearly 22% in the same months in the previous four years, according to EIA data.
CenterPoint estimates it will have to spend up to $20.5 million and take the plant offline for 14 weeks to make the repairs to keep the plant operating, according to the letter.

title: Deployable reserves shrinking as coal, gas forced outage rates rise: NERC
key_claim: Falling conventional availability is reducing deployable reserves, and battery storage cannot substitute during long-duration widespread events such as major winter storms.
frame_summary: Utility Dive is arguing that the reliability story in NERC's 2026 assessment is not a capacity shortfall but a shrinking deployable reserve, driven by ageing coal and combined-cycle units that were never designed for the cycling now demanded of them.
verbatim_quote: Demand growth and large load integration continue to challenge operators, NERC said.
